blocks.title: What Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) is
blocks.text:
Your Basal Metabolic Rate, or BMR, is the minimum amount of energy your body needs to keep its vital functions running at complete rest: breathing, blood circulation, temperature regulation, brain activity and cell renewal. Even if you spent the whole day lying down without moving, your body would still burn that energy.

BMR accounts for roughly 60% to 75% of total daily calorie expenditure. That makes it the starting point for any eating plan — whether you want to lose weight, maintain it or build muscle. Without knowing your BMR, any calorie target is guesswork.

blocks.title: How BMR is calculated
blocks.text:
This calculator uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, published in 1990 and considered the most accurate of the popular estimation formulas. It accounts for weight, height, age and biological sex:

• Men: BMR = 10 × weight (kg) + 6.25 × height (cm) − 5 × age (years) + 5
• Women: BMR = 10 × weight (kg) + 6.25 × height (cm) − 5 × age (years) − 161

The difference between men and women reflects the higher average proportion of lean mass in male bodies, which demands more energy at rest. The formula produces an estimate — for exact figures you would need indirect calorimetry testing in a lab.

blocks.title: BMR, TDEE and calorie burn: the difference
blocks.text:
These are three related but distinct numbers:

• BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate): what your body burns at complete rest, with no movement at all.
• TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure): what you actually burn given everything you do in a day — walking, working, training. It is calculated by multiplying BMR by an activity factor.
• Calorie target: how much you should eat to reach a specific goal. To lose weight, the target sits below your TDEE (a deficit). To gain weight, above it (a surplus).

Most people confuse BMR with TDEE. If you eat only your BMR you will create a deficit — but it may not be a healthy one, depending on your activity level. That is why this calculator shows all three figures.

blocks.title: What to do with this number
blocks.text:
Now that you have your BMR, your TDEE and a target per goal, the next step is adjusting how you eat:

• To lose weight: eat below your TDEE (the calculator suggests −20%, a moderate and sustainable deficit). Never go below the safety floor (1,500 kcal for men, 1,200 kcal for women) without professional supervision.
• To maintain: eat close to your TDEE. Swings of 100–200 kcal are normal and expected.
• To gain muscle: eat above your TDEE (+10% is a mild surplus that favors muscle gain with less fat storage).

Remember: these are estimates. The body is not a spreadsheet. Use them as a starting point, watch what happens on the scale and in the mirror over several weeks, and adjust. And whenever you can, work with a registered dietitian.

items.question: What is the difference between BMR and TDEE?
items.answer: BMR is what your body burns at complete rest — as if you stayed in bed all day. TDEE includes your BMR plus the energy spent on everything else you do (walking, working, training). TDEE is always higher than BMR.

items.question: How often should I recalculate my BMR?
items.answer: Recalculate whenever your weight changes significantly (5 kg or more), on each birthday (BMR declines with age), or when your activity level changes. In practice, once every 2–3 months is enough for most people.

items.question: Is the Mifflin-St Jeor formula accurate?
items.answer: It is the most accurate of the popular estimation equations, with a margin of error of about 10% for most of the population. Exact figures require indirect calorimetry testing. But for building a starting nutrition plan, it is more than good enough.

items.question: Can I eat less than my BMR to lose weight faster?
items.answer: It is not recommended. Eating consistently below your BMR can slow your metabolism and cause muscle loss, fatigue and nutrient deficiencies. This calculator already applies a safety floor (1,500 kcal for men, 1,200 kcal for women) to avoid that risk.

items.question: How do I count calories in practice without weighing everything?
items.answer: Use an app like Nutricalor: photograph your plate and the AI estimates calories and macros in seconds. It is far faster than weighing ingredients or searching through databases.

blocks.title: What a calorie deficit is
blocks.text:
A calorie deficit is when you consume fewer calories than your body burns. That gap forces your system to draw energy from its reserves — mainly body fat. It is the only proven mechanism for weight loss: whatever diet you follow, if it works, it works because it created a deficit.

The size of the deficit determines how fast you lose and how sustainable it is. Small deficits (10–15%) produce slow but comfortable loss, with less hunger and less risk of muscle loss. Large deficits (above 25%) speed things up but raise the odds of binge eating, fatigue and a metabolic plateau.

blocks.title: How to calculate your deficit
blocks.text:
The calculation has three steps:

1. Find your BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) — what your body burns at rest. This calculator uses the Mifflin-St Jeor formula, the most widely accepted one.
2. Multiply by your activity factor to get your TDEE (total daily burn): sedentary ×1.2, light ×1.375, moderate ×1.55, intense ×1.725.
3. Apply the deficit you want: subtract 10%, 20% or 25% from your TDEE. The result is your daily calorie target.

For example: if your TDEE is 2,400 kcal and you choose a moderate 20% deficit, your target lands at 1,920 kcal/day. The gap (480 kcal/day) adds up to 3,360 kcal over a week — roughly 0.44 kg of fat.

blocks.title: Which deficit is safe
blocks.text:
Research and clinical practice converge on a few limits:

• A deficit of 10–20% of your TDEE is considered safe and sustainable for most people. It is the range that preserves muscle mass, keeps your metabolism active and causes fewer side effects (excessive hunger, irritability, fatigue).
• A deficit above 25% can work in the short term, but it significantly raises the risk of binge eating, muscle loss and metabolic slowdown (the dreaded "plateau").
• Never go below the safety floor: 1,500 kcal/day for men and 1,200 kcal/day for women. Below that it is very hard to get all the micronutrients you need without medical supervision.

This calculator applies that floor automatically. If the deficit you pick would take you below the minimum, it adjusts and tells you.

blocks.title: How much you can actually lose per week
blocks.text:
The theoretical math is simple: every 7,700 kcal of deficit equals roughly 1 kg of fat. With a 500 kcal/day deficit, that works out to about 0.45 kg per week; at 250 kcal/day, about 0.23 kg.

In practice, though, the scale will swing more than that — and that is no reason to give up. Water retention, your menstrual cycle, the sodium in yesterday's dinner and even stress all affect daily weight. What matters is the trend across weeks.

A healthy, realistic pace for most people is between 0.3 and 0.7 kg per week. Losing faster is possible, but it usually costs you muscle and sanity. Slow and consistent wins.

items.question: Do I need to be in a deficit every single day?
items.answer: No. What matters is the weekly average. If you ate more at a celebration, pull back slightly over the following days — no drama. Consistency across weeks matters far more than daily perfection.

items.question: If I exercise more, can I eat more and still lose weight?
items.answer: In principle, yes. Exercise raises your TDEE, which allows a deficit with more food. But be careful: the calories burned in exercise are usually overestimated. Treat exercise as a tool for health and wellbeing, not as a license to eat without limit.

items.question: Is a light deficit for longer better than an aggressive one for a short time?
items.answer: For most people, a light to moderate deficit sustained for longer is more effective. Aggressive deficits produce fast early results but have a high dropout rate and a rebound effect. A deficit you can hold for months is worth more than one that lasts two weeks.

items.question: How do I count calories without weighing everything?
items.answer: Use an app like Nutricalor: photograph your plate and the AI estimates calories and macros in seconds. You do not need to weigh every ingredient — a photo estimate is practical enough to hold a deficit.

items.question: Does a calorie deficit work for everyone?
items.answer: A calorie deficit is the universal mechanism of weight loss. But the ideal size of the deficit, the composition of your diet and the rate of loss vary from person to person. Medical conditions (thyroid, insulin resistance, medications) can affect the process. Whenever possible, consult a registered dietitian.

blocks.title: How many calories should I eat per day
blocks.text:
How many calories you should eat per day depends on several factors: your current weight, height, age, biological sex and — above all — your daily activity level and your goal (lose, maintain or gain).

For most people there is no magic universal figure of 2,000 calories. A small, sedentary woman may need only 1,500 kcal, while a tall, very active man may need more than 3,000 kcal. That is why it is essential to use a personalized calculator that accounts for your physiology.

blocks.title: How we calculate your target
blocks.text:
We use a scientific method in three steps:

1. First we calculate your Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) using the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, which estimates the energy your body spends simply staying alive (breathing, circulation and so on).
2. Then we multiply your BMR by your activity factor (sedentary, light, moderate or intense) to find your Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE).
3. Finally we adjust that figure to your goal. To lose weight we apply a 20% deficit. To maintain, we keep the TDEE as is. To gain, we apply a 10% surplus.

blocks.title: Calories to lose, maintain or gain
blocks.text:
• To lose weight: the golden rule is a sustainable calorie deficit. We recommend cutting 20% from your daily burn. That delivers healthy weight loss without sacrificing muscle mass or leaving you hungry all the time. One caveat: we never suggest eating below the safety floor (1,500 kcal for men, 1,200 kcal for women).
• To maintain: ideal if you are already at your target weight, or if you want to focus on body recomposition (trading fat for muscle) at a slow pace.
• To gain: to build muscle (hypertrophy) you need a slight calorie surplus (around 10%) combined with strength training. Much more than that and the gain will be mostly fat.

blocks.title: Why calorie counting works (and how to make it easy)
blocks.text:
Whatever the diet of the moment — low carb, intermittent fasting, keto — the only biological reason it produces weight loss is that it creates a calorie deficit by the end of the day. Once you understand and track your calories, you get the freedom to eat the foods you enjoy, as long as they fit your daily target.

The worst part of counting calories has always been weighing every ingredient and digging through enormous databases. Nutricalor solves that with AI: you just take a photo of your plate, and the AI estimates the calories and macronutrients automatically — reading a full, mixed plate rather than a single labeled product.

items.question: Does the calorie target already include the exercise I do?
items.answer: Yes. The activity level you select already multiplies your basal rate to account for exercise. If you selected 'Moderate' or 'Intense', you do not need to add the calories burned in training separately — they are already in the figure.

items.question: Can I eat below 1,200 (women) or 1,500 (men) calories to speed things up?
items.answer: It is not recommended. Very low calorie diets (VLCD) can cause severe muscle loss, vitamin deficiency, extreme fatigue and hair loss. On top of that, when the diet ends, a slowed metabolism makes rapid weight regain more likely (the yo-yo effect).

items.question: If I hit my calories, does it matter what I eat?
items.answer: For the raw number on the scale, calorie quantity is the dominant factor. But for the quality of that weight (muscle vs fat), for satiety, health and energy, where those calories come from matters a great deal. You need enough protein, good fats, vitamins and fiber.

items.question: How do I know whether to focus on losing fat or building muscle?
items.answer: If your body fat percentage is high and it bothers you, losing fat should be the primary focus. If you are new to strength training, you can often build muscle and lose fat at the same time (body recomposition) by eating at maintenance or in a light deficit.

items.question: Does this calculator work for children and teenagers?
items.answer: No. This calculator (the Mifflin-St Jeor equation) has been validated only for adults (18 and over). Children and teenagers are still growing and have different metabolic needs, requiring pediatric or dietitian supervision.

blocks.title: What BMI is
blocks.text:
Body Mass Index (BMI) is a simple mathematical formula, created in the 19th century by the Belgian mathematician Adolphe Quetelet, that relates a person's weight to their height.

The World Health Organization (WHO) uses BMI as an international standard for quickly assessing whether an adult falls within a weight range considered healthy for their height, or whether they are underweight, overweight or living with obesity.

blocks.title: How to calculate BMI
blocks.text:
The BMI calculation is straightforward. You take your weight (in kilograms) and divide it by your height (in meters) squared.

The official formula is:

• BMI = weight (kg) ÷ (height (m) × height (m))

For example: someone who weighs 70 kg and is 1.75 m tall would calculate 70 ÷ (1.75 × 1.75) = 70 ÷ 3.06 = 22.8. That person would fall in the "Normal weight" range.

blocks.title: WHO classification table
blocks.text:
The World Health Organization classifies adult BMI (men and women aged 20 and over) into the following ranges:

• Below 18.5: Underweight
• Between 18.5 and 24.9: Normal weight
• Between 25.0 and 29.9: Overweight
• 30.0 or above: Obesity

blocks.title: The limits of BMI — why it doesn't tell the whole story
blocks.text:
While BMI is a useful epidemiological tool for assessing large populations, it has significant limitations when used on its own to assess an individual's health:

1. It does not tell muscle from fat: muscle is denser than fat. Athletes and very muscular people often get a BMI that labels them "overweight" or "obese" even with very low body fat and excellent cardiovascular health.
2. It does not assess fat distribution: visceral fat (stored in the abdomen, around the organs) is far more dangerous for metabolic health than subcutaneous fat (stored on the hips and thighs). Two people with the same BMI can have completely different cardiovascular risk profiles.
3. It does not account for age or ethnicity: the standard tables are not ideal for older adults (who naturally lose muscle and bone mass) or for pregnant women. Some populations, such as people of Asian descent, face metabolic risk at lower BMI values than the standard cut-off.

items.question: Does BMI work for children?
items.answer: BMI for children and teenagers (up to 19) uses the same formula, but the classification is different. Because they are still growing, the result must be compared against WHO-specific charts (percentiles), split by age and sex. This calculator was built for adults.

items.question: Is BMI different for men and women?
items.answer: No. For the World Health Organization's official adult classification, the table and cut-off points are the same for men and women.

items.question: My BMI says overweight — what now?
items.answer: BMI is only an indicator. A BMI in the overweight range does not automatically mean you are unwell. Look at other health markers, such as body fat percentage, waist circumference and blood work. Consult a professional for a full assessment.

items.question: Which matters more: BMI or body fat percentage?
items.answer: Body fat percentage is a far more accurate health indicator, because it reveals your body's actual composition (lean mass vs fat mass). BMI is used because it is much easier and cheaper to calculate than accurate body composition tests such as a DEXA scan or bioimpedance.

blocks.title: What macronutrients are
blocks.text:
Macronutrients, or "macros", are the three main components of food that supply energy to the body: protein, carbohydrates and fat. While vitamins and minerals (micronutrients) are needed in small amounts, macros are needed in large amounts (grams) every day.

Each macro plays an essential role:

• Protein: the building blocks of the body. Essential for building and repairing tissue (including muscle), producing enzymes and hormones, and supporting the immune system. (Provides ~4 kcal per gram.)
• Fat (lipids): fundamental for hormone health, absorbing fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K), protecting organs and storing long-term energy. (Provides ~9 kcal per gram.)
• Carbohydrates: the body's and the brain's preferred and fastest source of energy. (Provides ~4 kcal per gram.)

blocks.title: How to calculate your macros
blocks.text:
The macro split in this calculator follows an evidence-based standard for optimizing body composition (losing fat while keeping muscle, or gaining lean mass):

1. First we set total calories based on your BMR, activity factor and goal (lose, maintain or gain).
2. Protein: fixed at ~1.8 grams per kilogram of body weight. Several studies consider this the ideal amount for maximizing protein synthesis, whether you are in a calorie deficit or building muscle.
3. Fat: we reserve around 25% of daily calories for fat. That is enough to keep hormone production healthy.
4. Carbohydrates: the remaining calories go to carbs. They supply the energy you need for training and daily life.

blocks.title: Protein, carbs and fat: how much of each
blocks.text:
While the calculator gives you an excellent starting point, the ideal split can vary depending on your food preferences, genetics and type of training.

Endurance athletes (running, cycling) may need a higher proportion of carbohydrates, slightly reducing fat or protein. People with insulin resistance, or those who simply prefer higher-fat diets, can lower carbs and raise fat.

The main rule is: hit your calorie target and, to improve body composition, hit your protein target. The exact ratio between fat and carbs is less rigid and can be adapted to whatever you feel best following.

blocks.title: How macros change with your goal
blocks.text:
The beauty of calculating macros is the flexibility. Your body weight dictates protein, but your total calories — which dictate carbs and fat — change with your goal.

• Losing fat: protein stays high (crucial for not losing muscle mass), while carbs and fat come down to create the calorie deficit.
• Building muscle: you eat more calories overall. Protein stays sufficient (1.8 to 2.0 g/kg), but carbs increase significantly to fuel hard training and build new tissue.

items.question: Do I have to hit my macros to the gram every single day?
items.answer: No. Being perfectly exact is practically impossible. Focus on hitting your total calories within a margin (± 5–10%) and eating enough protein. If one day you eat slightly more carbs and slightly less fat, that is fine, as long as calories stay within range.

items.question: Won't eating fat make me gain weight?
items.answer: No. What causes weight gain is a total calorie surplus. Dietary fats (olive oil, avocado, nuts) are essential for your health and for producing hormones such as testosterone. The only thing to watch is the amount, since fat carries more than twice the calories (9 kcal/g) of protein and carbs (4 kcal/g).

items.question: Can I cut carbohydrates completely?
items.answer: The human body can survive without carbohydrates (through a process called ketogenesis), but most people feel much better, have more energy in training and stick to their diet more easily when they eat carbs in reasonable amounts. Cutting them entirely is unnecessary for weight loss.

items.question: Which macro matters most for strength training?
items.answer: Protein. Without it, the body cannot repair the microdamage caused by training and build new muscle fibers. That said, carbohydrates come second, since they supply the fuel you need to train hard.

items.question: How do I track macros practically day to day?
items.answer: By putting technology to work. With Nutricalor, instead of weighing everything on a scale and logging every gram, you simply photograph your plate. The AI estimates the macros from the food that is actually there, which makes tracking easy and sustainable over the long term.
